__readme: Shared parity fixtures for the ONE grading policy: the canonical resolved model in sdk/src/contract/grading-policy.ts, the normalization adapters that read it out of every contract that has expressed one, and the write adapter that turns an edit against it back into the PATCH settings the hosted API already accepts. Loaded by sdk/tests/contract-grading-policy.test.ts through sdk/tests/support/eval-grading-policy-fixtures.ts. It is written to be copied VERBATIM into mcpjam-backend as the G0b mirror corpus, exactly as eval-verdict-policy-parity-fixtures.json and score-contract-parity-fixtures.json already are: the backend cannot import @mcpjam/sdk into convex/ default-runtime code, so a shared fixture file is the only common ground truth. Copy it byte for byte; do not re-author it. LOAD RULE: strip EVERY key whose name starts with '__' before handing a row to a validator; they are fixture annotations (__label, __why) and every object in this contract is closed, so a payload still carrying them would be rejected for the wrong reason - turning an accept row into a false failure and, worse, a reject row into a false success. WHAT THIS CORPUS IS FOR. minimumAccuracy and passThreshold are NOT one number in two units: they differ in scope as well as units, so dividing a percent by 100 moves the bar for every suite with more than one case. The `scope` cohort is the proof (ten cases, nine always passing, one always failing: 90% suite-wide passes, 0.9 per-case fails), and every other cohort exists to stop some normalization from quietly picking one side of a divergence. THERE IS NO SINGLE LEGACY PRODUCER. Three shipped ones disagree in ways that decide runs: convex/testSuites.ts run finalization measures ITERATIONS and rates an empty run 1; convex/sdkEvals.ts computeEvalRunSummaryFromIterations measures CASES (variant-collapsed, absent cases dropped) and rates an empty run 0; sdk/src/eval-run-reporter.ts buildLocalFallbackResult measures the results it was handed and also rates an empty run 0. The `historicalSummaries` cohort pins all three against the same runs so that unifying the vocabulary cannot unify the arithmetic. COHORTS. `normalization`: an input contract plus the resolved policy it must produce; `input.source` is 'suiteFile', 'hostedSuite' or 'runReporting' and selects the adapter. `reject`: inputs that must be refused - `kind` is 'hostedSuite' (the adapter throws) or 'policy' (evalGradingPolicySchema refuses). `iterationResolution`: a rule, the per-case and per-run arguments, and the count resolveEvalGradingIterations must return. `thresholdConversion`: the only sanctioned fraction/percent conversion, pinned in both directions so IEEE-754 noise (0.07 * 100 = 7.000000000000001) never reaches the wire. `scope`: one run described as iteration rows, and what each criterion concludes about it. `historicalSummaries`: the same runs (by key into `runs`) under each of the three legacy producers, with the exact summary each must keep producing. `edits`: a policy (resolved from `policy`, the same shape as a normalization input), an edit, and the write plan planEvalGradingPolicyEdit must return. `rejectedEdits`: a policy and an edit the planner must THROW on. That is a different outcome from an ok:false refusal, and the split is deliberate: a refusal means this policy cannot express that operation, which a caller renders to a user, while a throw means the edit itself is malformed - an out-of-range number, a percent where a fraction belongs, an unknown field. EvalGradingPolicyEdit is a TypeScript type and TypeScript is not present at runtime, so a JavaScript caller, a CLI flag or an MCP argument can hand the planner anything; without the bound, passThreshold 90 plans minimumAccuracy 9000 on a suite-wide policy and reports success. ITERATION ROWS use testIteration.result's real vocabulary - pending, passed, failed, cancelled, timed_out - and nothing else. There is no evaluator-error result: a required scorer that errored lands as result: failed, and `evaluatorError: true` is a separate annotation that only the per-case contract's validity phase reads. That asymmetry is the point of the eight_evaluator_errors rows. THE THREE PROPERTIES THE `edits` COHORT EXISTS FOR. (1) The scope survives: a threshold edit writes minimumAccuracy on a suite-wide policy and passThreshold on a per-case one, and never the repetitions+passThreshold pair that applyVerdictPolicySettings reads as an upgrade. (2) An unchanged edit writes NOTHING: suite configRevision is a digest over the stored policy objects, so a read-edit-write round trip that re-sent them would rotate every suite's revision and invalidate its parity comparisons. (3) A refusal never degrades into a partial write: an edit carrying one unrepresentable field is refused whole, so a caller can never believe it set a count it did not set. NOT PINNED HERE: the per-case aggregation arithmetic and the inconclusive outcomes it produces, which eval-verdict-policy-parity-fixtures.json already owns. This corpus names per-case outcomes only where it contrasts them with a suite-wide one.

normalization.__why: A file's defaults are already canonical: a per-case FRACTION and a default count a case overrides. Omitted validity members resolve to the documented defaults, and the authored block stays empty so a write-back cannot materialize them.

normalization.__label: suite file, explicit minEligibleTrials replaces the coverage rule
normalization.__why: An explicit N is a WEAKER rule than omission: it tolerates unattempted trials. The resolved coverage therefore changes shape rather than gaining a number.

normalization.__label: suite file, explicit zero rates are not omissions
normalization.__why: `minCompletionRate: 0` asks for no completion floor; omitting it asks for 0.8. A `??` chain that treated 0 as absent would silently re-impose the default on a suite that opted out of it.

normalization.__label: suite file, unequal case counts and per-case thresholds
normalization.__why: Overrides survive with the case identity they were authored under; a case that overrides neither contributes no row, so an unchanged file cannot grow overrides by being read.
`verdictPolicyVersion: 2` plus `verdictPolicyDefaults` is the per-case policy. The stored `repetitions` is a DEFAULT, so a case override replaces it and may be lower.

normalization.__label: hosted suite, per-case storage, stale legacy columns are not read
normalization.__why: An upgrade leaves `defaultPassCriteria` and `minIterations` behind and nothing reads them. Projecting either into the policy would put a dead percent and a dead floor beside the live rule; the read DTO already reports `minimumAccuracy: null` for exactly this reason.

normalization.__label: hosted suite, per-case storage, empty stored validity reads as omitted
normalization.__why: `validity: {}` and an absent `validity` declare the same policy. They are kept DISTINCT in storage (the run snapshot writes the key only when the object is present) and the write adapter never turns one into the other, because an edit that changes nothing writes nothing.
The percent stays a percent, the floor stays a floor, and validity is NOT enforced: a suite-wide run is passed or failed and never inconclusive on evidence grounds.

normalization.__label: hosted suite, suite-wide storage with no declared threshold
normalization.__why: Every legacy producer spells the fallback `run.passCriteria?.minimumPassRate ?? 100`. It is a producer fallback, not a stored value, so reading it here changes no storage.

normalization.__label: hosted suite, suite-wide storage, floor clamped high
normalization.__why: `max(1, min(10, floor(value)))` is what `updateTestSuite`, `startTestSuiteRun` and the credit estimator all apply. Reporting the raw 42 would describe a floor no run uses.

normalization.__label: hosted suite, suite-wide storage, floor clamped low
normalization.__why: A stored 0 clamps to 1, which is the same as no floor in effect but is NOT `null`: the suite has a floor recorded, and an edit that clears it is a different write from one that leaves it alone.
An SDK run finalized by `sdkEvals.internalFinalizeSdkRun` is decided over CASES, with a fan-out run's provider/model rows collapsed into one bucket, and an empty population rated 0.

`EvalRunReporter`'s own summary counts the results it was handed, one per ITERATION. Same threshold, different denominator from the hosted ingestion above — which is why one member could not describe both.
Same `?? 100` producer fallback as a suite with no `defaultPassCriteria`.

reject.__label: per-case version with no stored defaults
reject.__why: The backend refuses to even estimate such a run (EVAL_VERDICT_POLICY_INCOMPLETE). Reading it as the suite-wide policy would decide its runs under semantics it never opted into, so the adapter throws instead of downgrading.

reject.__label: per-case version with a suite-wide threshold and no defaults
reject.__why: The presence of a legacy percent is not permission to fall back to it.

reject.__label: a suite-wide criterion carrying a per-case threshold override
reject.__why: Nothing reads a per-case threshold when the rate is measured once over the whole run, and the hosted API refuses to store one. Carrying it would render a bar that decides nothing.

reject.__label: a per-case criterion carrying a percent
reject.__why: thresholdPercent is not a key of the per-case member. A single object with both fields is how a fraction and a percent end up one refactor apart.

reject.__label: a per-case threshold expressed as a percent
reject.__why: 90 is out of [0,1]. The bound rejects the unit confusion structurally rather than in a refinement, so the failure names the field.

reject.__label: a suite-wide threshold expressed as a fraction
reject.__why: 0.9 is a legal percent (0.9%), so this one cannot be caught by a bound - which is exactly why the scope travels with the number instead of a caller guessing the unit. Rejected here only because emptyPopulationRate is missing.

reject.__label: a floor above the platform clamp
reject.__why: 11 is past the 1..10 range updateTestSuite enforces, so the model cannot describe a floor no run would apply.
1 is the floor of the portable range; a case that runs zero times is not a configuration.
enforced: true without declared and resolved is a claim with nothing behind it.
A suite with no validity phase cannot also declare one. This is the shape that would render an active 80% completion floor beside a legacy suite.

reject.__label: an empty-population rate that is neither 0 nor 1
reject.__why: The two shipped producers report exactly those two numbers. A third value would be a rule nobody implements.
The two names are the two shipped denominators. A new one is a new producer, not a spelling.
Origin is boundary metadata over a closed set of contracts, and a write adapter dispatches on it.
Every object here is strict, matching the Convex v.object the backend mirror uses.

iterationResolution.__why: The suite default is what a case runs.

iterationResolution.__label: default count, case override replaces it - downward
iterationResolution.__why: A default is REPLACED, not raised: the case runs 2, below the suite's 5. This is the half of the rule a floor does not have.

iterationResolution.__label: default count, run override wins outright
iterationResolution.__why: A transient per-run override beats both.

iterationResolution.__label: floor raises a smaller case count
iterationResolution.__why: max(case.runs, minIterations) - the case asked for 1 and runs 3.

iterationResolution.__label: floor never lowers a larger case count
iterationResolution.__why: The case asked for 7 and runs 7. Relabelling this floor a default count would silently cut the case to 3 - which is why an `iterations` edit against a floor rule is refused rather than written.

iterationResolution.__label: default count, case override replaces it - upward
iterationResolution.__why: A default is replaced in both directions: a case that asks for 7 gets 7, not the suite's 3. Nothing about a default count is a floor.

iterationResolution.__label: the contrast: a legacy case at runs 7 under a floor of 3
iterationResolution.__why: Pair one of two. The case's own count under a floor rule is testCase.runs, and the floor raises it: 7.

iterationResolution.__label: the contrast: the same legacy case under a default count of 3
iterationResolution.__why: Pair two of two, and the reason converting a floor into a default count is a policy change rather than a relabelling. A per-case rule reads testCase.REPETITIONS, a different column, which a legacy case does not have - so the same case resolves to the suite default 3 and loses four of its seven iterations. The two rules are not two spellings of one number.
A missing case count is 1 before the floor applies, matching Math.max(1, Math.floor(runs ?? 1)).
null is no floor at all; the case count stands.

iterationResolution.__label: no floor and no case count
iterationResolution.__why: Both absent still resolves to the producer's 1.
A replay re-executes its source run's snapshotted counts (!useSnapshotTests && ...), so a floor added after that run does not retroactively raise it.

iterationResolution.__label: replay still honours a run override
iterationResolution.__why: The override is computed before the replay branch and wins either way.

iterationResolution.__label: replay is a no-op under a default count
iterationResolution.__why: A per-case run freezes its expected trial identities into the verdict-policy snapshot at run start, so there is no floor for a replay to skip.

iterationResolution.__label: floor and case count both at the cap
iterationResolution.__why: 10 is the clamp ceiling for the floor; a case may configure more and keeps it.

scope.__label: ten cases, nine always passing, one always failing
scope.__why: THE counterexample. A 90% suite-wide threshold passes this run; a 0.9 per-case threshold fails it, because case_10 passes 0 of its 1 iteration. Dividing 90 by 100 does not preserve the policy - it moves the bar for every suite with more than one case.

scope.__label: the same shape with three iterations per case
scope.__why: 27 of 30 iterations and 9 of 10 cases both come to 0.9, so the two suite-wide populations agree here and still disagree with per-case. Equal case sizes are what make the two populations coincide; the next row removes that.

scope.__label: unequal case sizes split the two suite-wide populations
scope.__why: One passing iteration out of ten is 10%; one passing case out of two is 50%. At a 50% threshold the ITERATION population fails this run and the CASE population passes it - the same stored percent, two shipped producers, opposite answers.

scope.__label: one case fanned across two models
scope.__why: iterationGroupKeyForSummary does not key on the execution variant, so both models collapse into ONE case bucket and a single failure fails it: 0 of 1 case, against 3 of 6 iterations. The per-case contract keys a case aggregate on (caseId, executionVariant) and reports the two models separately, which is the third answer.

scope.__label: a held iteration is in the iteration denominator and absent from the case one
scope.__why: A pending row (a run still held in grading) lowers the iteration rate to 0.9 and drops out of the case population entirely, because a case with no terminal iteration is `absent` and is never counted. The same run is 90% to one producer and 100% to the other.

scope.__label: a cancelled iteration stays in the iteration denominator
scope.__why: Cancellation is NOT withdrawn from a suite-wide denominator the way the per-case contract withdraws it: the row is still one of ten iterations. Under the case population case_2 has no terminal iteration and is dropped instead.

scope.__label: a timed-out iteration is a FAILURE under both suite-wide producers
scope.__why: result === 'failed' || result === 'timed_out' is the shipped failure test, so a timeout counts against the run rather than dropping out of it. This is the one non-passing lifecycle outcome the two populations agree on.

The empty-population rate is the whole difference: the hosted finalizer rates an empty run 1 and passes it at any threshold; the SDK ingestion and local fallback rate it 0 and fail it at every threshold above 0.

scope.__label: eight evaluator errors and two passes
scope.__why: Eight iterations whose REQUIRED evaluator errored. testIteration.result has no evaluator-error member, so a failing required scorer lands as result: failed and every suite-wide producer reads it as the server failing: the rate is 0.2 and the run FAILS. Under the per-case policy the same run is INCONCLUSIVE - an 0.8 evaluator-error rate is over the 0.1 ceiling, read from metadata the suite-wide producers never consult - and that outcome is unreachable for a suite-wide suite, which has no validity phase at all.
scope.perCaseNote: inconclusive: evaluatorErrorRate 8/10 = 0.8 exceeds the resolved 0.1 ceiling, so validity does not hold and no task verdict is reached. The per-case arithmetic is pinned in eval-verdict-policy-parity-fixtures.json; it is named here only to contrast the two scopes.

scope.__label: a measured assertion failure is not an evaluator error
scope.__why: Three iterations the grader judged and found wanting. Every suite-wide producer reads them as failures, and the per-case policy reads them as a measured 0.0 pass rate rather than as missing evidence: validity holds and the case FAILS. An evaluator that errored on the same three would produce no task verdict at all.

edits.__label: per-case: a threshold edit writes passThreshold
edits.__why: The fraction goes to the fraction field. minimumAccuracy is never written on a per-case suite - the route refuses it outright, and converting it would be a percent no run uses.

edits.__label: suite-wide: a threshold edit writes minimumAccuracy
edits.__why: Same canonical fraction, converted at the boundary to the percent this suite's producer reads, over the population it already measured. passThreshold is NOT written, and neither is repetitions - which is what stops a threshold edit from migrating the suite.

edits.__label: suite-wide: a threshold edit restating the stored value writes nothing
edits.__why: 0.9 is the stored 90. An unchanged edit produces an EMPTY patch, so a read-edit-write round trip sends no policy field and cannot rotate the suite's configRevision.

edits.__label: per-case: a threshold edit restating the stored value writes nothing
edits.__why: The same property on the fraction side.

edits.__label: per-case: an iteration-count edit writes repetitions
edits.__why: A default count is a real field on this policy, so the canonical count edit is representable.

edits.__label: per-case: an iteration-count edit restating the stored value writes nothing
edits.__why: Unchanged is unchanged on the count side too.

edits.__label: suite-wide: an iteration-count edit is REFUSED
edits.__why: There is no suite default count under a floor rule. Writing 7 as minimumIterations would raise every case that configured less and lower nothing - a different policy from the one asked for - so the edit is refused and names settings.minimumIterations as the operation that does exist.

edits.__label: suite-wide: a threshold AND count edit is refused WHOLE
edits.__why: The anti-migration row. Dropping the unrepresentable count and writing the threshold would look like a success; sending repetitions with passThreshold is exactly the pair applyVerdictPolicySettings reads as an upgrade. Neither happens: the plan carries no settings at all.

edits.__label: per-case: a floor edit is REFUSED
edits.__why: A per-case suite has no iteration minimum. Writing minimumIterations onto it would store a floor the per-case resolver never reads, leaving a number in the settings sheet that decides nothing.

edits.__label: suite-wide: setting a floor where there was none
edits.__why: null to 3 is a change, and it writes the field the platform already has.

edits.__label: suite-wide: clearing a floor
edits.__why: null is forwarded verbatim because the platform reads null as clear and undefined as leave-alone; collapsing them would turn every attempt to remove the floor into a silent no-op.

edits.__label: suite-wide: a floor edit restating the stored value writes nothing
edits.__why: 3 is already stored.

edits.__label: suite-wide: a floor edit matching the CLAMPED stored value writes nothing
edits.__why: Storage holds 42, which the platform clamps to 10, so the floor in effect is 10 and an edit to 10 changes nothing. The comparison is against the resolved (clamped) value, not the raw column, so a suite whose stored floor predates the route's bound does not rotate its revision on a no-op edit.

edits.__label: suite-wide: a validity edit is REFUSED
edits.__why: This suite has no validity phase: its runs cannot be inconclusive. Turning that on changes what a run may conclude, so it is a reviewed grading-policy change and not a settings edit - and sending validity alone to the route would be rejected anyway, with a message about repetitions and passThreshold that does not describe what was asked.

edits.__label: per-case: a validity edit writes the declared change
edits.__why: Merge semantics, matching the route: the caller adjusting one ceiling did not ask to clear the others.

edits.__label: per-case: a validity edit restating the declared value writes nothing
edits.__why: 0.9 is already declared.

edits.__label: per-case: declaring minEligibleTrials where it was omitted IS a change
edits.__why: Omission selects the stricter all-configured-attempted rule; an explicit 1 selects the eligible-count rule instead. The two resolve to different coverage kinds, so comparing the declared blocks is the only comparison that sees it - a resolved-policy comparison would call this a no-op and drop the write.

edits.__label: per-case: declaring the resolved default rate IS a change
edits.__why: An omitted minCompletionRate resolves to 0.8, but declaring 0.8 pins it against a future default change. The declared block is what round-trips, so the write happens.

edits.__label: an empty edit writes nothing, per-case
edits.__why: No field mentioned, no field written.

edits.__label: an empty edit writes nothing, suite-wide
edits.__why: The same on the other side.

edits.__label: a reported run's policy refuses every edit
edits.__why: passCriteria travelled with one run and has no settings write path. Refusing names the suite as the thing to edit instead of writing a percent onto a run that is already decided.

edits.__label: suite-wide: float noise never reaches the wire
edits.__why: 0.07 * 100 is 7.000000000000001 in IEEE-754. Writing that would render as 7.000000000000001% and would make the next unchanged comparison report a change forever.

edits.__label: suite-wide: a fractional percent survives
edits.__why: 90.5% is a legal stored percent and 0.905 is its fraction. The conversion is exact in both directions, so this edit is a no-op against a suite already at 90.5.

rejectedEdits.__label: a percent where a fraction belongs, suite-wide
rejectedEdits.__why: passThreshold is ALWAYS a fraction on this API; the adapter converts to the stored percent. Accepting 90 would plan minimumAccuracy: 9000, which the route rejects - a successful plan the API then refuses.

rejectedEdits.__label: a percent where a fraction belongs, per-case
rejectedEdits.__why: The same input on the other scope plans passThreshold: 90, out of the route's [0,1].

rejectedEdits.__label: a floor above the platform range
rejectedEdits.__why: The route bounds minimumIterations to 1..10. Silently clamping 42 to 10 would report an edit as applied that was not the edit asked for, so it is refused instead.

rejectedEdits.__label: a floor below the platform range
rejectedEdits.__why: 0 is not 'no floor' - null is. The route refuses 0 and so does the planner.
The floor is an integer count of iterations.

rejectedEdits.__label: a default count above the portable maximum
rejectedEdits.__why: MAX_REPETITIONS bounds the count in the suite file, the route and the contract alike.
A case that runs zero times is not a configuration.

rejectedEdits.__label: a validity rate out of range
rejectedEdits.__why: minCompletionRate is a fraction like every other rate in this contract.
An explicit floor of 0 would be 'no coverage requirement', which omission does NOT mean and the schema does not allow.
The edit shape is strict: a misspelled field silently doing nothing is how a caller believes it set something it did not.
